Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 11: ‘“God blessed the seventh day [and sanctified it]” – Rabbi Yishmael said: He blessed it with manna and He sanctified it with manna. He blessed it with manna in that all the days of the week one omer [of manna] would fall, while on the day before Shabbat two omers would fall. for Shabbat. He sanctified it with manna, as it did not fall on it [on Shabbat] at all. Rabbi Natan says: He blessed it with manna and sanctified it with a blessing. Rabbi Yitzḥak said: He blessed it with manna and sanctified it through the gatherer. He blessed it with apparel. Rav Huna said: He should change his clothing. Rabbi Ḥiyya said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan: He should mix [garments]. Avin bar Ḥisdai said:…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 1 — Bereishit and the Three Foundations of Creation, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 11) to illuminate his statement here (“just as we find (Bereishit Rabbah, parashah 11) regarding everything that was created during the six days of Creation, " terms such as 'the Work of Creation' and the like, everything being designated by the name...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And even though this was merited by advancing "we will do" before "we will hear", which might imply that it was earned through "we will do" alone—the truth is the reverse; for surely had they uttered this impulsively, without inward heartfelt contemplation and sober balance of mind, this would not have been accounted to the praise of "we will do", since it would have stemmed merely from a lack of emotional equilibrium.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 47:1–4
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it.” And it is stated in Midrash Rabbah (Bereishit 11:2): He blessed it with the manna—for on all weekdays one omer fell per person, and on Friday two omers; and He sanctified it with the manna—for none descended on Shabbat at all. And the nature of the manna is, as taught in Pirkei Avot (5:6), that it was created at twilight, meaning that it harmonizes this physical world and the supernal world; and on Shabbat a direct bond is likewise forged linking the lower realm to the supernal realm.

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: All the supernal Sefirot and garments of creation were contracted (tzimtzum) solely so that finite human beings could receive the light of the Torah step by step without being overwhelmed, transforming every veil of concealment into a mirror through which the heart comes to know its Creator.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Tikkunei Zohar 21a:1-24a:2: ‘For there are fifty gates of freedom, with Her, corresponding to the fifty times, that the ‘Exodus from Egypt’ is mentioned in the Torah. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: The measure of a person’s wisdom in Oral Torah determines the power of his prayer. These two voices repair the eating from the Tree of Knowledge: Oral Torah is drawn from that side, and from it comes the voice of prayer. Prayer is rabbinic in institution; for from the absolute apprehension that “there is nothing besides Him,” where all is one, what place is there for prayer?
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Deuteronomy, Ki Teitzei 9
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “When you go forth to war against your enemies, and the Lord your God delivers them into your hand” (Deuteronomy 21:10): the entire life of man in this world is a campaign to rescue the sparks of holiness held captive by the inclination, and when a person goes forth in the name of Heaven, the Blessed Name delivers his adversaries into his hand.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: So that even if he cannot conquer it through Torah reflection (unholy thoughts disturbing his study); the preceding derech eretz remains to subdue it through natural moral decency. And so even when the yetzer deceives him into thinking his frequent intimacy is for the sake of Heaven to dispel stray thoughts; according to his perspective he acts within derech eretz, wherefore it is called "like roosters" regarding natural conduct; yet it is derogatory, being merely the way of physical man without holiness!

And the explanation is that this awe encompasses everything, and among all created beings, there is none who does not revere this. (Dover Tzedek 31a, s.v. "U'lefikhad").

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Nedarim 20a: ‘§ It is taught in a baraita: “That His fear may be upon your faces” (Exodus 20:17); this is referring to shame, as shame causes one to blush. “That you not sin” (Exodus 20:17) teaches that shame leads to fear of sin. From here the Sages said: It is a good sign in a person that he is one who experiences shame. Others say: Any person who experiences shame will not quickly sin, and conversely, one who does not have the capacity to be shamefaced, it is known that his forefathers did not stand at Mount Sinai.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 1 — Bereishit and the Three Foundations of Creation, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Nedarim 20a) to illuminate his statement here (“And it is brought (Nedarim 20a): "' ''That His fear may be upon your faces' – this refers to shame, ' 'so that you do not sin, etc.,' any man who possesses shame will not readily sin.' And it is taught (at the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: The theme: Shabbat issuing from the treasury of fear of Heaven, perceiving the Divine Presence on Shabbat, and wisdom existing only when rooted in the heart. Hashem said: "I have a precious gift in My treasury". In Berachos (33b), the Sages declare: "The Holy One has nothing in His treasury save the storehouse of fear of Heaven (yir'at Shamayim), as it is said: The fear of Hashem is His treasure (Yeshayah 33:6)". Perforce, Shabbat is drawn from that very treasury!
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 70:21–24
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As written (Exodus 20:17): “and that His fear may be before your faces, that you sin not,” explained in Nedarim (20a): this is shame. And as in the Zohar (Terumah 135a): from the Written Torah we derive the Oral Torah, for the Oral Torah is likewise the aspect of awe. So here when Adam entered slumber, his transcendent vitality ascending—the pristine love and certainty in Hashem who brought him into the world— there remained in him the attribute of awe which is the female principle, as written: “a woman that fears the Lord, she shall be praised,” this being the creation of the female through the deep slumber.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him, requested that they perform lovingkindness with him in selling a burial plot (Bereishis 23); and all the people of his town and his neighbors had certainly absorbed a glimmer of his virtues; but it was merely from the lips outward, even though they protested: "hear us, my lord: you are a mighty prince among us; none of us shall withhold from you his sepulchre" (ibid. 23:6); and so Ephron declared with his mouth: "a piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between me and you?" Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And from Hashem’s vantage point, it is as taught in the Talmud (Chagigah 12a): “At the time the Holy One, blessed be He, created His world, it expanded continuously like two balls of warp-threads,” meaning that from Hashem’s side existence expands boundlessly without limit or end; and when Hashem uttered “Let there be,” it kept expanding, and only for the sake of the vessel of creation did Hashem say “Dai” (Enough!), thereby imposing these finite borders.

And the dynamic of this warfare operates through the intensity of awe, as taught (Berakhot 28b): that through the fear of Heaven matching the fear of flesh and blood one desists from committing a transgression; functioning through shame before the Blessed Name, which is the zenith of awe, as written in Nedarim (20a): "'that His fear may be upon your faces, that you sin not'—this refers to shame".
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 62:4–6
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As taught in Tractate Nedarim (20a): “‘That His fear may be before your faces, that you sin not’ (Exodus 20:17)—this refers to shame.” And in this attribute there are two expressions: The first expression is wholly virtuous: namely, that a person feels shame before his Creator to do what is evil in His sight.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 28b: ‘His students said to him: Our teacher, bless us. He said to them: May it be His will that the fear of Heaven shall be upon you like the fear of flesh and blood. His students were puzzled and said: To that point and not beyond? Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For divine awe functions like tzitzit, through which one reaches "do not spy out after your own heart", by recognizing one's dignity when attired in garments of honor as mentioned above, so operates the fear of Heaven hovering upon a person's countenance. And our Sages expounded (Nedarim 20a) on "that His fear may be upon you": this is shame/modesty (boshet); and this connects to what they taught (Berakhot 28b): when a person sins he thinks: "if only no man sees me", which stems from shame before the sight of flesh and blood.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Numbers, Matot 4
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Regarding the request of the tribes of Reuben and Gad across the Jordan: whenever a person sanctifies his place within the four cubits of halakhah (cf. Berakhot 8a) and yearns to connect his portion with the Sanctuary, he draws the sanctity of the Land of Israel even into the outer territories so as to elevate and refine them.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Psalms 111:10: ‘The beginning of wisdom is reverence toward GOD;all who practice it gain sound understanding.Praise of [God] is everlasting.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 1 — Bereishit and the Three Foundations of Creation, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Psalms 111:10) to illuminate his statement here (“as it is stated (Psalms 111:10): 'The beginning of wisdom is the fear of Hashem,' and it is written (Proverbs 1:7): 'The fear of Hashem is the beginning of knowledge,' for this represents the ultimate intention...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Yet nevertheless this reverent trembling is the essential catalyst, and as written: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of Hashem, etc." (Psalms 111:10), and as written: "What does Hashem your God ask of you but to fear, etc." (Deuteronomy 10:12), and "the Holy One, blessed be He, has nothing in His world except the treasure of the fear of Heaven, etc." (Berakhot 33b); for this is what reminds and arouses the sleeping heart to repent.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 37:44–46
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Wherefore David proclaims: “A good understanding have all they that do thereafter” (Psalms 111:10)—making room for a fellow’s viewpoint. As in Zohar Beshalach (51b): “‘And the middle bar in the midst of the boards’—this is the Holy One; Rabbi Yitzchak said: this is Jacob, all being one”; the wise man recognizing that judgment lies concealed within the smiling face of the King, exercising holy caution (see below, section 38).

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 7
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: "I have lifted up my hand unto Hashem, etc." (Genesis 14:22). The reason Avraham our Father refused to benefit from the king of Sodom, even though we find that he accepted gifts from Pharaoh and Avimelech, was because his going to rescue Lot required spiritual justification and refinement; for within Lot there resided a spark of holiness, inasmuch as Na'amah the Ammonitess and Ruth the Moabitess were destined to be born of him, while the remainder was corrupt, giving rise to Ammon and Moab as explained; and he had to demonstrate that his innermost intent was exclusively to salvage those two righteous scions (Bava Kamma 38b).

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 54:1–3
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And now nothing will be withholden from them, which they purpose to do.” In Midrash Rabbah (38:9): This teaches that the Holy One opened for them a portal of repentance, as said: “And now (ve'atah)”—and “ve'atah” signifies repentance, as it is said (Deuteronomy 10:12): “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you, but to fear”; yet they said “No”; whereupon the Holy One declared: “Nothing shall be cut off/withheld from them that they purpose to do.”

So too is the beginning of the Torah: "I am Hashem your God, etc.," for it is impossible to arrive at "You shall have no other gods, etc."—the rejection of evil— except through the prior recognition of "I am, etc."
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Tiferet Yosef, Noach 1:4
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And concerning the concept of the “worlds that were destroyed,” as taught in the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 9:2): “This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, created worlds and destroyed them, saying: ‘These do not please Me, but this one pleases Me.’” And in truth, how can such an idea apply to Hashem — that He should create worlds and subsequently need to destroy them? Is it not written concerning Him (Isaiah 46:10): “Declaring the end from the beginning”!

Section_Title: Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 3 — The Threefold Sanctity of Vayechulu
Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Targum Jerusalem on Genesis 2:2: ‘In Targum Yerushalmi on Genesis 2:2, the word va-yekhal (“and He finished”) is rendered va-chamid (“and He desired / cherished,” from the root kalah, yearning of the soul, as in “My soul yearns [kaltah] for Your salvation”); and Abudarham notes that for this reason the Sabbath prayer calls Shabbat chemdat ha-yamim (“the coveted / cherished of all days”).’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: By linking va-yekhal to divine yearning and delight (va-chamid / chemdat ha-yamim), Rav Tzadok shows that the first occurrence of ‘on the seventh day’ expresses Hashem’s love and longing for Knesset Yisrael, who would receive the Torah on Shabbat.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the root objective of the Torah is the striving and intellectual initiative to innovate and to "walk before Him," not resting solely upon received tradition; and through this he draws down light by forming renewed souls as though he created them, for the root of souls is itself the root of the Torah, as is known. And its inception from "and the souls, etc."— these were converts whom he brought under the wings of faith, yet none of their lineage endured within the covenant.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Tiferet Yosef, Bereshit 1:6–7
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And likewise it is stated in the Holy Zohar (Tetzaveh 184a): “There is no true light except that light which emerges out of darkness.” That is to say: precisely because Hashem set before man such dense garments, to the extent that it can seem to him that he can act against His will, and yet man, through his divine service, pierces through every kind of concealing garment — this is the ultimate triumph, and this is what is termed “turning oneself consciously toward the good.”

Section_Title: Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 3 — The Threefold Sanctity of Vayechulu
Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 9:4: ‘In the Torah scroll of Rabbi Meir they found written on “And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good (tov me’od)” (Genesis 1:31): “and behold, death was good”—and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman said: “Behold, it was very good” refers to the Evil Inclination (Yetzer HaRa), as well as suffering and Gehinnom, for through them man is spurred to return to God.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok connects the word kol (‘from all [mi-kol] His work’) in the second clause of Vayechulu with the word kol in Genesis 1:31 (‘all [et kol] that He had made, and behold, it was very good’): through the Torah given on Shabbat, even the forces that appear opposite to goodness—such as the Evil Inclination—are ultimately transformed into ‘very good.’
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the final letter Hei, in the rectification of the element of water, shines on the Seventh Day of Pesach, when He submerged our adversaries in the waters and led Israel through the sea on dry land, "and the waters were a wall unto them on their right hand, and on their left" (Shemos 14:22); so that the immersion of carnal desires held no dominion over them, becoming on the contrary a shielding wall and refuge on every side; after the manner of what is said (Bereishis Rabbah 9:7): "'and behold, it was very good' (Bereishis 1:31)—this refers to the yetzer hara".
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 45:1–3
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And God saw everything that He had made, and, behold, it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day.” It is stated in Midrash Rabbah (Bereishit 9:2): This teaches that the Holy One was building worlds and destroying them, saying: “This one pleases Me, those did not.” And to understand this: surely the Blessed Name does not create something merely to destroy it!

Section_Title: Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 3 — The Threefold Sanctity of Vayechulu
Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 1:31: ‘And God saw all (et kol) that He had made, and behold, it was very good (tov me’od).’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: While each individual day’s creation was pronounced ‘good’ (tov), the all-encompassing vista of ‘all that He had made’ (et kol asher asah)—which includes the adversarial forces of darkness and the Evil Inclination—is pronounced ‘very good’ (tov me’od) when rectified through the Torah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Descending and enticing the woman until he succeeded in becoming subsequently the Angel of Death. Nevertheless all was for the ultimate good and as an authentic aid; and had they merited to conquer the tempting yetzer then, they would have ascended to an incomparably higher summit; and though they did not merit this and brought about generational weeping, not being vindicated in their judgment on that first Rosh Hashanah and sentenced to death; nonetheless they merited the continuation of their seed, the great chain of the Patriarchs of the world and Knesset Israel from generation to generation.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 7:16–17
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And it is taught in the Holy Zohar (Bo 39b) and cited by Rashi (Genesis 1:1): Rabbi Yitzchak said: The Torah should not have begun except from “This month shall be unto you”; yet the Midrash Rabbah (Bereishit 1:2) and Rashi explain: on account of “He declared the power of His works to His people, to give them the heritage of nations” (Psalms 111:6).

Section_Title: Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 3 — The Threefold Sanctity of Vayechulu
Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Isaiah 45:7: ‘I form light and create darkness; I make peace and create evil (u-vorei ra); I the Lord do all these things.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Scripture explicitly testifies in Isaiah 45:7 that the Creator Himself formed darkness and evil so that they may ultimately serve the revelation of light and peace.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And even Pharaoh's defiance: "Who is Hashem that I should obey His voice?", having been inscribed in the Torah, reflects his vital root wherein God embedded this challenge, for cosmic concealment likewise proceeds from Hashem's essential will in Creation: first darkness and then light (Shabbat 77b); and "forming light and creating darkness" Isaiah 45:7, creation (Beri'ah) being an exalted realm, darkness stemming from a deeper divine desire that darkness serve a purpose.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 31:4–6
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And for this reason it is written: “And there was evening”—denoting the divine constriction—and only afterward “and there was morning.” And as my revered father, my master and teacher, of blessed memory, explained: on account of this principle Scripture states (Isaiah 45:7): “Former of light and Creator of darkness,” which seemingly is astonishing: why is “formation” (yetzirah) written regarding light and “creation” (beriah) regarding darkness, when Beriah is spiritually higher than Yetzirah, as stated in the Holy Zohar (Terumah 155a)?

Section_Title: Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 3 — The Threefold Sanctity of Vayechulu
Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 11b: ‘In the prophet Isaiah it is written: “Who forms light and creates darkness, who makes peace and creates evil” (Isaiah 45:7); yet in the morning blessing before Shema we recite: “Who makes peace and creates all things (ha-kol),” employing a refined, euphemistic expression (lishna ma’alya).’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok points out that the Talmud’s substitution of ha-kol (‘all things’) for ra (‘evil’) in Berakhot 11b is not merely verbal politeness: it reveals that the word kol (‘all’) in ‘He rested from all (mi-kol) His work’ specifically encompasses the opposite of good, which is elevated into holiness through the Torah of Shabbat.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Likewise, all the varieties of vegetation created on the third day grow from one earth; they are one at their source even though their growth branches into separate forms. This is the meaning of 'He prepared the world for His congregation': the world was prepared for this apprehension and this praise.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 37:18–23
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Therefore the Zohar states that Above there is no connective Vav; no labor being needed Above to unite opposites, all standing in serene clarity; descending below, however, they appear as conflicting opposites, wherefore they shattered upon entering human grasp. And because Hashem desired that harmony be forged from man's side as well, as in Berakhot (11b): mentioning the attribute of day at night and night during day — the second Tablets were given with the connective Vav, training man never to overreach in any single trait.

Section_Title: Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 3 — The Threefold Sanctity of Vayechulu
Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Or HaChaim on Genesis 2:2:1: ‘Rabbi Chaim ibn Attar (Ohr HaChaim on Genesis 2:2–3) explains that during the six days of Creation, the Holy One, blessed be He, endowed the universe with only enough spiritual life-force to endure for six days; when Shabbat arrives, the Creator infuses a new soul and fresh vitality into the world on every Shabbat, empowering creation to exist for another six days—and this is the meaning of “And God blessed the seventh day,” that it continually generates blessing and existence for the six workdays.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok cites the Ohr HaChaim to explain the third mention of ‘the seventh day’ (‘And God blessed the seventh day’): because ‘blessing’ (berakhah) always signifies increase and reproduction, the blessing of Shabbat—activated by Israel’s acceptance of the Torah on Shabbat—continually gives birth to the spiritual vitality of the six ensuing weekdays.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And throughout all the Ten Days of Repentance unfolds the learning of inner strategies how to wipe away stains and become purified from all iniquities on Yom Kippur, wherein the intrinsic essence of the day atones, scours, and wipes clean. And every spiritual phenomenon exists across "World (Space), Year (Time), and Soul": in Soul—the High Priest corresponds to Yom Kippur, as written in Sefer Yosippon that they titled him 'the atoner for his congregation'; and in World (Space)—it is the Altar.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 8:19–22
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Hence the Blessed Name created darkness so that man through his toil should forge light out of darkness; and through Israel restraining their physical desires, they illuminate their souls and achieve clear recognition of their Creator. And this is what is written: “He declared the power of His works to His people, to give them the heritage of nations” — meaning that the Blessed Name revealed to them even the light that transcends their natural grasp—the hidden lights of the six days of creation—so that through Israel's service darkness turns into light.

Section_Title: Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 3 — The Threefold Sanctity of Vayechulu
Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 89b: ‘In the Time to Come, the Holy One, blessed be He, will say to Isaac: Your children have sinned against Me! Isaac will reply before Him: Master of the Universe, even if a person lived seventy or eighty years, how many years could he actually sin once sleep, childhood, prayer, and bodily needs are subtracted? And if You will bear the sin, bear it all! Thereupon Israel will declare to Isaac: “For You are our father!” and Rava expounded: “Though your sins be as scarlet (ka-shanim), they shall become white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18)—even if your sins are ingrained like these years (shanim) that have been ordered and continuous from the six days of Creation until now, they shall become white as snow!’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok maps the three clauses of Vayechulu onto the three supernal heads of Shabbat: Va-yekhal corresponds to the Friday night meal of Chakal Tapuchin Kadishin (Malkhut, revealing that Israel’s souls are intrinsically pure ‘apples’); Va-yishbot mi-kol melakhto corresponds to the Sabbath day meal of Atika Kadisha (Keter, the primordial utterance of Bereishit), where through repentance out of love even the sins ordered from the six days of Creation (‘ka-shanim’) are whitened into snow and revealed as part of the primordial design.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: This is what is written in Perek Rabbi Akiva (Shabbat 89b): "'though your sins be as scarlet (kashanim)'—these are like the cosmic years (kashanim) that have been ordered and advancing since the six days of Creation"; meaning that thus they were preordained in the primordial Thought of Creation during the six days of Genesis; and when this is clarified through the unveiling of the letters of Thought; then "they shall be as white as snow" (Yeshayah 1:18), all the sins of Israel being clarified as mentioned.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 17:10 (§2)
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: For so it is brought in the writings of the holy Ari: that there were many spiritual giants who walked in Hashem's ways with integrity yet never grasped their essential source and root. And this is the mystery of Isaac, as brought in the Talmud (Shabbat 89b): Isaac said to them: “Rather than praising me, praise the Holy One, blessed be He,” and Isaac pointed out the Holy One directly before their eyes.

Section_Title: Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 3 — The Threefold Sanctity of Vayechulu
Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Zohar, Vayikra 2:10: ‘At the beginning of Parashat Vayikra (Zohar III 2a), the letter Vav (whose numerical value is six) is expounded as the “Sign of Truth” (Ot Emet), corresponding to Ze’ir Anpin (the Holy One, blessed be He, and the attribute of Jacob), which channels supernal blessing into the six directions of the world.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok links the third clause (‘And God blessed the seventh day’) to the third Sabbath meal (Seudah Shelishit), corresponding to Ze’ir Anpin—the letter Vav, the ‘Sign of Truth’—which draws the eternal truth of Shabbat into the six days of the coming week.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And sin is governed by human free choice. And indeed, the classical dilemma of Foreknowledge (Yedi'ah) and Free Choice (Bechirah) is known, which they resolved in Zohar Chadash and in the book Arba Me'ot Shekel Kesef of the Arizal according to the esoteric wisdom; and the root of the matter is: they dwell in two distinct spiritual dimensions, and in the realm of Foreknowledge there is in truth no place for free choice; except that this is the transcendent dimension concealed in this world, destined to be revealed in the Future when the yetzer hara is purged and free choice is truly nullified.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 7:6
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: There it is written (Zohar Shemot, 135b), “the word baruch in barchu brings forth blessing from the source of life, the place which brings forth all saturation to water everything [which is Yesod of Binah. Sulam]. Since it is the source from where God’s abundance flows forth in the secret of the sign of the brit milah [Yesod of Zeir Anpin] it is called ‘hamevurach [blessed],’

Section_Title: Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 3 — The Threefold Sanctity of Vayechulu
Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 12:19: ‘The lip of truth shall be established forever (sefat emet tikon la’ad), but a lying tongue is but for a moment.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Because Ze’ir Anpin (the attribute of Jacob and the Written Torah, represented by the letter Vav) is the attribute of Truth (‘You give truth to Jacob’), the blessing drawn down from Shabbat through Vayevarekh endures forever and sustains the six weekdays in holiness.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Thus physical matter is the true illusion, "falsehood" denoting that which lacks permanence: "The lip of truth shall be established forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment" [Proverbs 12:19]; "falsehood" (kazav) meaning something that terminates, as in "whose waters fail not (lo yechazvu)" [Isaiah 58:11]. Wherefore worldly passions are termed "falsehood": "Bread of deceit (shaker) is sweet to a man" [Proverbs 20:17] [and note the precision of the Holy Tongue: the matriarch of lust in the desert was named Cozbi (Kozbi), signifying deception].
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 12:1–4
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “Noah was a righteous man.” In Tanchuma (Nitzavim 1): This is what Scripture says (Proverbs 12:7): “The wicked are overthrown, and are not; but the house of the righteous shall stand” — whenever the Holy One scrutinizes the deeds of the wicked and overturns them, they have no remedy; He overturned the deeds of the Flood generation and they had no survival, as said: “and He blotted out all existence”; Israel, however, falls and rises, as said: “Rejoice not against me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall arise”; therefore it is said: “The wicked are overthrown and are not, but the house of the righteous shall stand.”

Section_Title: Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 3 — The Threefold Sanctity of Vayechulu
Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Psalms 111:6: ‘He has declared to His people the power of His works (koach ma’asav higid le-amo), in giving them the heritage of the nations’ (Psalms 111:6)—cited by Rashi on Genesis 1:1 from Midrash Tanchuma and Bereshit Rabbah 1:2 to explain why the Torah opens with the account of Creation. Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok explains why the Divine Name Elohim (‘Master of all forces,’ ba’al ha-kochot kulam) appears three times in Vayechulu: in Va-yekhal Elohim and Va-yevarekh Elohim, the Name Elohim signifies that even the human awakening from below (itaruta de-letata) by which Israel sanctifies Shabbat is itself a power granted to Israel by Hashem.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Then automatically the Land of Israel will be subdued before them. And this is the meaning of Psalms 111:6: "The power of His works He told to His people, to give them the heritage of the nations": and our Sages expounded in Bereishit Rabbah 1 and Tanchuma: for this reason He told them what was created on the first day, the second day, etc.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 12:11–13
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And the Midrash Rabbah (Bereishit 1:2) resolves: on account of “He declared the power of His works to His people, to give them the heritage of nations” (Psalms 111:6), in that the Blessed Name recorded this so that Israel should have connection even to the lofty holiness of the Patriarchs. For although Israel arose in divine thought at the inception, nevertheless from their own side they possess connection only within the realm of conscious labor, where intellect functions.

Section_Title: Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 3 — The Threefold Sanctity of Vayechulu
Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Yoma 69b: ‘In the morning liturgy (and cf. Yoma 69b on the Men of the Great Assembly restoring God’s crowns): “You were He (Atah Hu) before the world was created; You are He (Atah Hu) since the world was created”—signifying the absolute, unchanging unity of Atika Kadisha above all division between good and evil.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In the middle clause—‘and He rested (va-yishbot) on the seventh day from all His work’—the Name Elohim is omitted! Rav Tzadok explains that this is because the rectification of ‘from all His work’ (transforming evil itself into good) stems from Atika Kadisha, the transcendent realm of ‘You were He before the world was created,’ where no opposing force ever existed independently.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Whereas the trial of David HaMelech with a Jewish woman did not succeed for him, for the “blood” of that trial was for “transforming,” not for “subduing,” since in truth she was fitting for him, and this is not the level of Yosef. And the essential distinction between Israel and the nations is in the sign of the covenant — which is why “orlah” is named for the nations.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Genesis, Lech Lecha 3
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: "And God said unto Avraham: And as for you, you shall keep My covenant, you, and your seed after you throughout their generations" (Genesis 17:9). The reason Avraham did not observe the mitzvah of circumcision before being commanded, whereas we find in the Gemara (Yoma 28b): 'Avraham our Father observed even Eruv Tavshilin'; is that indeed, all other commandments serve as a protective guard for man so that he walk in accordance with 'God made man upright' (Ecclesiastes 7:29), and not swerve to an extreme, but proceed along the balanced path; for if one becomes excessively immersed in a single pursuit, he will distort the straight path and stray from it…

Section_Title: Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 3 — The Threefold Sanctity of Vayechulu
Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 2:3: ‘And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it; because that in it He rested from all His work which God created to make (asher bara Elohim la’asot).’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: The third occurrence of the Name Elohim appears at the very end of Vayechulu—‘which God (Elohim) created to make (la’asot)’—teaching that when the transcendent light of Atika descends into the lower world of Elohim, it empowers human beings (‘to make’) to transform darkness into light.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the first time the word "holiness" (kedushah) is mentioned in the Torah is in connection with the Sabbath day, immediately at the creation of the world in Parashat Bereishis: "And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it" (Bereishis 2:3); and I received by tradition from Bereishis Rabbah a fundamental principle: in the place where a word is mentioned for the first time in the Torah, there lies the essential root of that matter.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 29:66–70
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And why at the dawn of creation the Name Elohim alone is mentioned, whereas later when the sprouts stood poised at the threshold of the soil it states (Genesis 2:5): “For the Lord God (Havayah Elohim) had not caused it to rain” — the reason is that Elohim represents strict judgment and structural causality; and when Hashem willed to emanate the world He set up a prime cause—the Name Elohim, meaning “Master of all powers”— through which all worlds cascaded by strict cause and effect.
